Individual measurements collected from mature specimens in the lower Amazon basin indicate that the ultimate total length of Psectrogaster rutiloides reaches approximately 17.8 centimeters [Li = approximately 17.8 centimeters], a size that positions this species among the medium-bodied members of its genus. Field records from multiple sampling expeditions have demonstrated that this maximum length is attained only after several years of sustained growth, with asymptotic body size being achieved relatively late in the species' ontogeny. In contrast, the total length at which individuals first become capable of reproducing is considerably smaller; morphometric analyses of gonadal development have established that puberty occurs at a body length of roughly 9.6 centimeters [Lp = roughly 9.6 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to a notable shift in somatic investment priorities.

Reproductive studies conducted under controlled laboratory conditions at a constant water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] have provided detailed insights into the fecundity schedule of this characiform. Females produce a mean of 149113 eggs per annual spawning cycle [Ri = 149113 eggs per annual spawning cycle], with a single spawning event occurring each year [F_R_i = single spawning event occurring each year]; this aggregate annual output represents the maximum reproductive rate observed for the species. The thermal regime of 25 °C appears to be optimal for gametogenesis and spawning coordination, as deviations from this temperature have been associated with reduced clutch sizes and asynchronous reproductive activity in related curimatid species.

The early developmental stages of Psectrogaster rutiloides are characterized by remarkably low initial mass and rapid transition to exogenous feeding. The wet weight at birth, calculated from egg diameter measurements averaging 1.34 millimeters, is approximately 0.0013 g [Wwb = approximately 0.0013 g], placing the species among the smallest neonatal sizes recorded for Neotropical freshwater fishes. This minimal birth mass necessitates a very brief period of endogenous nutrition, and embryos maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] complete yolk-sac absorption and initiate first exogenous feeding after roughly 7.5 days [ab = roughly 7.5 days]. The short duration of the lecithotrophic phase is interpreted as an adaptation to warm, productive environments where planktonic prey is consistently available, allowing for rapid transition to a fully feeding larval existence.

Adult body composition data compiled from extensive field collections reveal that the attainable wet weight of mature individuals reaches a maximum of 147.62 grams [Wwi = 147.62 grams], representing the upper size limit documented for this species across its geographic range. This ultimate mass is achieved only by the largest and oldest individuals and is consistent with the asymptotic body size predicted from length-weight regressions. At the onset of reproductive competence, corresponding to the 9.6 centimeter pubertal length threshold, the corresponding wet weight at puberty averages approximately 21.1 grams [Wwp = approximately 21.1 grams], indicating that individuals must allocate substantial somatic growth between the attainment of sexual maturity and the achievement of their full adult mass potential.

Longevity estimates derived from otolith increment analysis and mark-recapture studies, conducted under the thermal conditions typical of the species' natural habitat (25 °C [T = 25 °C]), suggest that the maximum lifespan of Psectrogaster rutiloides is approximately 18 years [am = approximately 18 years]. This extended lifespan, comparable to that documented for the related characiform Astyanax mexicanus, positions the species as a relatively long-lived member of its family. The substantial time between the age at first exogenous feeding and reproductive maturity, combined with multiple years of adult reproductive activity, underscores a life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic persistence and iteroparous reproduction over a single, high-investment spawning event.
